messages.author: cffcce570e30f29d
messages.subject: Improving Code Efficiency (Discrete Choice Analysis)
parts:
Continuing my learning and exploration of RStan via the Discrete Choice analysis. Here is the code that Daniel Guhl and Sebastien Gabel developed. I tried to change the code to be vectors rather than use the loop statements. But the changes I made failed. I'm wondering if some one can suggest the correct modifications

Krishna

data {
  int<lower=1> N;                                 // number of choice sets
  int<lower=1> K;                                 // number of parameters (utility)
  int<lower=1> D;                                 // number of parameters (beta)
  int<lower=2> J;                                 // number of alternatives
  int<lower=1> I;                                 // number of respondents
  int<lower=1,upper=J> y[N];                      // alternative selected
  int<lower=1,upper=I> id[N];                     // respondent index
  matrix[J,K] x[N];                               // array of design matrices
  matrix[I,D] d;                                  // matrix of demographics
}

parameters {
  matrix[D, K] mu;                                // means for beta
  matrix[K, I] alpha;                             // std normal draws
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;                // cholesky factors
  vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[K] tau_unif;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,K] beta;                               // utility parameters (individual level)
  cholesky_factor_cov[K] L;                       // cholesky factors
  vector[J] v[N];                                 // utility vector for each choice set
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;                         // scale

  for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);

  L = diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);

  beta = d * mu + (L * alpha)';                   // individual level parameters

  for (n in 1:N) {
    v[n] = x[n] * beta[id[n]]';
  }
}

model {
  to_vector(alpha) ~ normal(0, 1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);                 // lkj prior
  to_vector(mu) ~ normal(0, 10);                  // prior for mean parameters

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~ categorical_logit(v[n]);
  }
}

generated quantities {
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;                            // cov matrix
  real<upper=0> log_lik;                          // log_lik for each sample

  Sigma = tcrossprod(L);

  log_lik = 0;
  for (n in 1:N) {
    log_lik = log_lik + categorical_logit_lpmf(y[n] | v[n]);
  }
}

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: Improving Code Efficiency (Discrete Choice Analysis)
parts:
Hi,

First, RStan can use quite a bit of memory, especially when you are running a complex model. Have you monitored your computer's memory use when you start the model? 

Assuming the issue is RAM usage, one solution is to avoid saving parameters you don't care about or can re-construct. I am guessing this bit is causing RStan to save a lot of parameters like that.

transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,K] beta;                               // utility parameters (individual level)
  cholesky_factor_cov[K] L;                       // cholesky factors
  vector[J] v[N];                                 // utility vector for each choice set
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;                         // scale

  for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);

  L = diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);

  beta = d * mu + (L * alpha)';                   // individual level parameters

  for (n in 1:N) {
    v[n] = x[n] * beta[id[n]]';
  }
}

Moving this to the "model" section will result in them not being saved in the output, and should reduce the memory usage of the model.

Second, is there a reason you are running 20,000 iterations? While this can be the default in JAGS, it is probably overkill for Stan by an order of magnitude. Saving that many samples might also cause issues with memory usage.

Lastly, if you really need to record thousands or tens of thousands of variables but are not running on a machine with a lot of RAM, you might explore cmdstan, as it saves the results to disk rather than in memory. For me, running a fairly complex model with 30,000 observations in cmdstan will rarely use more than 0.5 GB RAM per chain.

Hope that helps,

Matt

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: Improving Code Efficiency (Discrete Choice Analysis)
parts:
100% memory usage is definitely no good.

If you move those parts to the model section, they will not be saved in the output. However, everything in the transformed parameters is determined by your parameters and data, so you could extract the parameters at the end of the model run, and then in R calculate each of the transformed parameters. It is definitely a bit of work, and just saving what the model calculates is certainly the easiest path. But it is a good trick to avoid saving intermediate variables you are not concerned about, or if you are trying to reduce the size of the output.

As for using Cmdstan, the cmdstan guide has a great getting started section which should get you most of the way there. The only slightly tricky thing is preparing the data. For this, I get the data prepared in R similar to using Rstan, and then use the Rstan function stan_rdump() to save all the data to a file that cmdstan can read. After the run, you will have a .csv which can be read into R using the RStan function read_stan_csv(). From there everything is pretty much the same as working with the output of RStan.

I always start running a model in Stan with 200 warmup, 200 samples per chain, and then increase if it appears I need better warmup or more N_eff. In my experience, with 4 chains and a straightforward, well identified model this typically is more than enough.
 
Matt

On Monday, October 17, 2016 at 12:33:26 PM UTC-4, Matt Espe wrote:
100% memory usage is definitely no good.

If you move those parts to the model section, they will not be saved in the output. However, everything in the transformed parameters is determined by your parameters and data, so you could extract the parameters at the end of the model run, and then in R calculate each of the transformed parameters. It is definitely a bit of work, and just saving what the model calculates is certainly the easiest path. But it is a good trick to avoid saving intermediate variables you are not concerned about, or if you are trying to reduce the size of the output.

As for using Cmdstan, the cmdstan guide has a great getting started section which should get you most of the way there. The only slightly tricky thing is preparing the data. For this, I get the data prepared in R similar to using Rstan, and then use the Rstan function stan_rdump() to save all the data to a file that cmdstan can read. After the run, you will have a .csv which can be read into R using the RStan function read_stan_csv(). From there everything is pretty much the same as working with the output of RStan.

I always start running a model in Stan with 200 warmup, 200 samples per chain, and then increase if it appears I need better warmup or more N_eff. In my experience, with 4 chains and a straightforward, well identified model this typically is more than enough.
 
Matt

Hi,

First, RStan can use quite a bit of memory, especially when you are running a complex model. Have you monitored your computer's memory use when you start the model? 

Assuming the issue is RAM usage, one solution is to avoid saving parameters you don't care about or can re-construct. I am guessing this bit is causing RStan to save a lot of parameters like that. 

transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,K] beta;                               // utility parameters (individual level)
  cholesky_factor_cov[K] L;                       // cholesky factors
  vector[J] v[N];                                 // utility vector for each choice set
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;                         // scale

  for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);

  L = diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);

  beta = d * mu + (L * alpha)';                   // individual level parameters

  for (n in 1:N) {
    v[n] = x[n] * beta[id[n]]';
  }
}



Moving this to the "model" section will result in them not being saved in the output, and should reduce the memory usage of the model.

Second, is there a reason you are running 20,000 iterations? While this can be the default in JAGS, it is probably overkill for Stan by an order of magnitude. Saving that many samples might also cause issues with memory usage.

Lastly, if you really need to record thousands or tens of thousands of variables but are not running on a machine with a lot of RAM, you might explore cmdstan, as it saves the results to disk rather than in memory. For me, running a fairly complex model with 30,000 observations in cmdstan will rarely use more than 0.5 GB RAM per chain.

Hope that helps,

Matt
